info.bio:
Small Faces fue un grupo musical británico fuertemente influenciado por el rhythm'n'blues americano,  fundado en 1965 y liderado por el guitarrista y cantante Steve Marriott y el bajista Ronnie Lane, ambos coautores de la mayoría de las canciones de la banda. Ian McLagan al órgano (en sustitución del teclista Jimmy Winston en 1966) y el baterista Kenney Jones completaban la formación. 

Se convirtieron en uno de los grupos psicodélicos más exitosos de Inglaterra antes de su ruptura a finales de la década de los sesenta

own_scenes.desc: El único grupo mod que salió del público al escenario y a las listas: tres Top 10 y un álbum Top 3 en 1966 entre pop, acordes a lo Who, rave-ups y groove de Stax, culminados por «All or Nothing», número 1 en septiembre. Presentados como cockneys pícaros, una boy band mod paseada por Don Arden, en mayo de 1966 Brian Epstein les dio naranjas con LSD y nada volvió a ser igual. «My Mind’s Eye» (noviembre, número 4 en diciembre), con la melodía del villancico «Angels We Have Heard on High», era claramente una canción de drogas («mind» era palabra clave), aunque la prensa británica no se enteró: un orgullo de outsider que ve lo que los demás no ven. Arden filtró la maqueta a la radio y el grupo rompió con él. «Pensar es una pasada», decía Marriott; Ronnie Lane: la vida debía tener algo más.

refs.q: ‘My Mind’s Eye’ was clearly a drug song
refs.para: ‘My Mind’s Eye’ was clearly a drug song, although it said much for the comparative naivety of the British music press and record-buying public that this wasn’t fully realised in late 1966. Like ‘dream’, the term ‘mind’ had become a keyword for the psychedelic experience: a gateway into the interior, subjective states brought on by the use of marijuana and LSD. Nothing could have been more different from the pill-fuelled clubbing and frantic consumerism that marked the Small Faces’ early career and the whole idea of Swinging London.
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: In late 1966, LSD was the great divider: between those who were and those who weren’t in the know.
refs.para: In late 1966, LSD was the great divider: between those who were and those who weren’t in the know. Pop was becoming a battleground of warring tribes: between the hippies, the teenyboppers and the mums and dads; between those who wanted to progress, those who wanted everything to stay in the present and those who wanted to hark back to the past. Records were becoming indicators of an attitude, even of a world view. Yesterday, today or tomorrow: what was it to be?
refs.chapter: Diciembre: My Mind’s Eye: sueños de libertad, una minoría profética y el regreso a la infancia

refs.q: Steve Marriott nailed his colours to the mast that December.
refs.para: Steve Marriott nailed his colours to the mast that December. ‘I agree the old “groupy” world is tottering,’ he told Rave, ‘and I’m sad for those who have to go.’ But he felt that the pop scene had never been more exciting, after Revolver and the Beach Boys had spurred everyone on to higher and higher standards. ‘I’m very serious about it,’ he said. ‘It is an art, whether people wish to admit it or not. There is a whole new outlook in sound now, not around the corner but on the corner … you must be a musician, and a thinker.

scenes.name: Rock progresivo
scenes.author: Piero Scaruffi
scenes.desc: Al emigrar a Gran Bretaña, el rock se convierte en mercancía de moda pero también se descontextualiza: lo que en EE UU era el diario de la juventud se vuelve en Gran Bretaña un ensayo. El progresivo no comenta la cultura juvenil sino que busca la innovación técnica: arranca con las óperas rock (S.F. Sorrow, Tommy) y los álbumes conceptuales, lo cimentan Traffic, Jeff Beck, Jethro Tull, Family y Genesis, y alcanza su cima con King Crimson (In The Court Of The Crimson King), Van Der Graaf Generator y Yes. Colosseum, la Third Ear Band (inventores de la world music), las variantes góticas (High Tide, Black Widow) y folk (Comus, Strawbs), Gentle Giant, Emerson Lake & Palmer y Roxy Music, que revoluciona el género y prepara la new wave y el synth-pop.

xref.title: Small Faces Became Faces When Rod Stewart and Ronnie Wood Joined – Both Later Became Rock Royalty
xref.body: When Steve Marriott left the Small Faces in 1969 to form Humble Pie, the rest of the group hired a new guitarist and a new singer. The guitarist was Ronnie Wood, who six years later would replace Mick Taylor in the Rolling Stones. The singer was a gravel-voiced former grave digger named Rod Stewart. The name changed from Small Faces to simply the Faces — because the two tall new members made the "small" descriptor irrelevant. "The new guitarist was Ronnie Wood. Six years later he'd replace Mick Taylor in the Rolling Stones."

srcs.source: The Ongoing History of New Music
